+## What
+
+Implement a prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.

+## Why
+
+To evaluate my software engineering abilities.
+
+## Details
+
+This is a design of a project, hereafter known as Jobs, that will comprise the all the pieces of a job worker service.
+
+### Architecture
+
+The Jobs project will be comprised of two deliverables:
+
+1. A server (known as `jobd`)
+2. A client (know as `jobctl`)
+
+#### jobd
+
+The main logic of `jobd` will be isolated in a reusable Go package called `jobs`. It will be located under `<repo_root>/pkg/jobs` to encorage reuse. 
+
+##### `jobs` package
+
+The `jobs` package will implement an API with the following methods:
+
+* `Start`: Start a new job. This method accepts a string-based command (and an optional slice of arguments) and returns a `JobID` (a unique identifier for the job). The JobID will generated by reading a value from `/proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid`.
+* `Stop`: Stop a running job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Status`: Get the status of a job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Output`: Get the stdout and stderr of a job's process. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+
+To reduce complexity, the `jobs` package will maintain all state in memory:
+
+* The jobs will be held in a map that is keyed by `JobID`.
+* Job output will be persisted to a field on the Job itself. In order to support clients that join mid-stream, a custom writer will be needed that uses a multiwriter to write output to all clients but also tracks the full output so that can it be prepended to the stream for new clients. +func newOutputWriter(ww io.Writer) *outputWriter {
+	w := &outputWriter{
+		mu:      &sync.RWMutex{},
+		storage: &strings.Builder{},
+	}
+
+	w.Add(ww)
+
+	return w
+}
+
+type outputWriter struct {
+	mu      *sync.RWMutex
+	w       io.Writer
+	storage *strings.Builder
+	writers []io.Writer
+}
+
+func (w *outputWriter) Add(ww io.Writer) {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+
+	ww.Write([]byte(w.storage.String()))
+	w.writers = append(w.writers, ww)
+	w.w = io.MultiWriter(append(w.writers, w.storage)...)

+## What
+
+Implement a prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Why
+
+To evaluate my software engineering abilities.
+
+## Details
+
+This is a design of a project, hereafter known as Jobs, that will comprise the all the pieces of a job worker service.
+
+### Architecture
+
+The Jobs project will be comprised of two deliverables:
+
+1. A server (known as `jobd`)
+2. A client (know as `jobctl`)
+
+#### jobd
+
+The main logic of `jobd` will be isolated in a reusable Go package called `jobs`. It will be located under `<repo_root>/pkg/jobs` to encorage reuse. 
+
+##### `jobs` package
+
+The `jobs` package will implement an API with the following methods:
+
+* `Start`: Start a new job. This method accepts a string-based command and returns a `JobID` (a unique identifier for the job).
+* `Stop`: Stop a running job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Status`: Get the status of a job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Output`: Get the stdout and stderr of a job's process. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+
+To reduce complexity, the `jobs` package will maintain all state in memory:
+
+* The jobs will be held in a map that is keyed by `JobID`.
+* Job output will be persisted to a field on the Job itself. In order to support clients that join mid-stream, a custom writer will be needed that uses a multiwriter to write output to all clients but also tracks the full output so that can it be prepended to the stream for new clients.
+* Jobs will be run in their own goroutine. A `context.Context` will need to be stored on the Job to make sure that jobs can be easily canceled.
+* All resource isolation and control will be handled by the `jobs` package. Basic control levels (CPU, RAM, and disk IO) will be configurable when the job is started.
+* The jobs manager will run all jobs on the host machine. There will be no support for additional worker nodes.
+* Once a Job is complete, 
+
+Ideally, the `jobs` package will be a complete process execution manager.
+
+##### Process Execution Lifecycle
+
+Each job that is requested will go through the following lifecycle:
+
+* The manager will create a root cgroup (if it doesn't already exist) at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs`. This will be the parent cgroup for all jobs that run.
+* The manager will create a job-specific cgroup at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs/<job-id>`.
+* All job-specific limits will be applied to the child cgroup.
+* A new mount namespace will be created for the job (using `syscall.PivotRoot`, `syscall.Mount`, etc).
+* The manager will spawn a new process and run the command.
+
+This lifecycle will be run in a dedicated goroutine for each command that is run. The manager will pass a `context.Context` into the goroutine and keep a reference to it so that it can stop the job at any point.
+
+##### gRPC API
+
+`jobd` will also have a gRCP API (located at `internal/api`). This API will, as closely as possible, mirror the interface of the `jobs` package.
+
+Additional features:
+
+* mTLS support: The repository will contain pre-generated, self-signed certs that can be used by `jobd` (as well as `jobctl`). These certs will be used to authenticate any clients that connect. A simple gRCP interceptor will be needed to implement this.
+* Choosing a set of cypher suites with recent versions of Go (and TLS 1.3) is [not possible](https://go.dev/blog/tls-cipher-suites). In order to get the benefits of TLS 1.3, I'm going to use the recommended cypher suites. For reference: ECDHE, ECDSA, AES, and SHA are the most efficient and secure choices for KEX, auth, encryption, and MAC.
+* Authorization: Clients will be required to pass a gRCP metadata header indicating a client name. The server will maintain a hardcoded list of valid names and authenticate the client name against this list. This will also be handled in a gRCP interceptor.
comment.body:
Since we are using mTLS, the simplest approach would be to take the common name from the client's certificate subject. For now, let's call the value in `CN` the "username". 

The server will maintain a hardcoded list of valid usernames. One cert per username will be generated ahead of time with the `CN` set to the username (simulating a production environment where this would be controlled). 

When the user authenticates, their CN becomes their authorization in the system. The gRPC server can check this username against the hardcoded list.

+# RFD 1 - Design
+
+## What
+
+Implement a prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Why
+
+To evaluate my software engineering abilities.
+
+## Details
+
+This is a design of a project, hereafter known as Jobs, that will comprise the all the pieces of a job worker service.
+
+### Architecture
+
+The Jobs project will be comprised of two deliverables:
+
+1. A server (known as `jobd`)
+2. A client (know as `jobctl`)
+
+#### jobd
+
+The main logic of `jobd` will be isolated in a reusable Go package called `jobs`. It will be located under `<repo_root>/pkg/jobs` to encorage reuse. 
+
+##### `jobs` package
+
+The `jobs` package will implement an API with the following methods:
+
+* `Start`: Start a new job. This method accepts a string-based command and returns a `JobID` (a unique identifier for the job).
+* `Stop`: Stop a running job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Status`: Get the status of a job. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+* `Output`: Get the stdout and stderr of a job's process. This method accepts a `JobID`.
+
+To reduce complexity, the `jobs` package will maintain all state in memory:
+
+* The jobs will be held in a map that is keyed by `JobID`.
+* Job output will be persisted to a field on the Job itself. In order to support clients that join mid-stream, a custom writer will be needed that uses a multiwriter to write output to all clients but also tracks the full output so that can it be prepended to the stream for new clients.
+* Jobs will be run in their own goroutine. A `context.Context` will need to be stored on the Job to make sure that jobs can be easily canceled.
+* All resource isolation and control will be handled by the `jobs` package. Basic control levels (CPU, RAM, and disk IO) will be configurable when the job is started.
+* The jobs manager will run all jobs on the host machine. There will be no support for additional worker nodes.
+* Once a Job is complete, 
+
+Ideally, the `jobs` package will be a complete process execution manager.
+
+##### Process Execution Lifecycle
+
+Each job that is requested will go through the following lifecycle:
+
+* The manager will create a root cgroup (if it doesn't already exist) at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs`. This will be the parent cgroup for all jobs that run.
+* The manager will create a job-specific cgroup at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs/<job-id>`.
+* All job-specific limits will be applied to the child cgroup.
+* A new mount namespace will be created for the job (using `syscall.PivotRoot`, `syscall.Mount`, etc).
+* The manager will spawn a new process and run the command.
+
+This lifecycle will be run in a dedicated goroutine for each command that is run. The manager will pass a `context.Context` into the goroutine and keep a reference to it so that it can stop the job at any point.

+2. A client (know as `jobctl`)

+
+The `jobs` package will implement an API with the following methods:

+* Job output will be persisted to a field on the Job itself. +func newOutputWriter(ww io.Writer) *outputWriter {
+	w := &outputWriter{
+		mu:      &sync.RWMutex{},
+		storage: &strings.Builder{},
+	}
+
+	w.Add(ww)
+
+	return w
+}
+
+type outputWriter struct {
+	mu      *sync.RWMutex
+	w       io.Writer
+	storage *strings.Builder
+	writers []io.Writer
+}
+
+func (w *outputWriter) Add(ww io.Writer) {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+
+	ww.Write([]byte(w.storage.String()))
+	w.writers = append(w.writers, ww)
+	w.w = io.MultiWriter(append(w.writers, w.storage)...)
+}

+	w.mu.RLock()
+	defer w.mu.RUnlock()
+
+	return w.w.Write(p)
+}
+

+	w.mu.RLock()
+	defer w.mu.RUnlock()
+
+	return w.storage.String()

+// they would be added to the writer. The Add function would bring late clients

+* The jobs manager will run all jobs on the host machine. There will be no support for additional worker nodes.

+* Job output will be persisted to a field on the Job itself. In order to support clients that join mid-stream, a custom writer will be needed that uses a multiwriter to write output to all clients but also tracks the full output so that can it be prepended to the stream for new clients. An implementation would look something like this:
+```go
+func newOutputWriter(ww io.Writer) *outputWriter {
+	w := &outputWriter{
+		mu:      &sync.RWMutex{},
+		storage: &bytes.Buffer{},
+	}
+
+	w.Add(ww)
+
+	return w
+}
+
+type outputWriter struct {
+	mu      *sync.RWMutex
+	storage *bytes.Buffer
+	writers []chan []byte
+}
+
+func (w *outputWriter) Add(ww io.Writer) {
+	w.mu.Lock()
+	defer w.mu.Unlock()
+
+	ch := make(chan []byte, 100)
+
+	go func() {
+		ww.Write(w.storage.Bytes())
+		for b := range ch {
+			ww.Write(b)
+		}
+	}()
+
+	w.writers = append(w.writers, ch)
+}
+
+func (w *outputWriter) Write(p []byte) (int, error) {
+	w.mu.RLock()
+	defer w.mu.RUnlock()
+
+	n, err := w.storage.Write(p)
+	if err != nil {
+		return n, err
+	}
+
+	for _, ch := range w.writers {
+		select {
+		case ch <- p:
+		default:
+		}
+	}
+
+	return n, nil
+}
+
+func (w *outputWriter) Storage() string {
+	w.mu.RLock()
+	defer w.mu.RUnlock()
+
+	return w.storage.String()
+}
+
+// The server would keep one outputWriter for each job. As clients connected,
+// they would be added to the writer. The Add function would bring late clients
+// up to date by writing the storage value first while everything else was blocked.
+```
+* Jobs will be run in their own goroutine.
+* All resource isolation and control will be handled by the `jobs` package. Basic control levels (CPU, RAM, and disk IO) will be configurable when the job is started.
+* The jobs manager will run all jobs on the host machine. There will be no support for additional worker nodes.
+
+Ideally, the `jobs` package will be a complete process execution manager.
+
+##### Process Execution Lifecycle
+
+Each job that is requested will go through the following lifecycle:
+
+* The manager will create a root cgroup (if it doesn't already exist) at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs`. This will be the parent cgroup for all jobs that run.
+* The manager will create a job-specific cgroup at `/sys/fs/cgroup/jobs/<job-id>`.
+* All job-specific limits will be applied to the child cgroup. The following hardcoded values will be used: `memoryMax: "32M"`, `cpuMax: "20000 100000"`, and `ioMax:"<MAJ:MIN> rbps=1048576 wbps=1048576"` (where `<MAJ:MIN>` will be determined by running `lsblk -o MAJ:MIN` and taking the whole disk).
+* A new mount namespace will be created for the job (using `syscall.PivotRoot`, `syscall.Mount`, etc).
